title: Optimisation: where the derivative is zero
intro: A company maximizes profit, a model minimizes its loss. On a smooth function an extremum can only sit where the slope vanishes: \( f'(x) = 0 \). This topic: critical points, first and second derivative tests, checking the edges — and gradient descent when algebra stalls.
keyPoints: Extrema of a smooth function on a closed interval can only sit at critical points (\( f'(c) = 0 \) or \( f' \) does not exist) or on the boundaries of the domain — nowhere else.
First-derivative test: if \( f' \) switches from + to − at a critical point it is a local maximum; from − to + a local minimum; no sign change, no extremum (like \( x^3 \) at 0).
Second-derivative test: \( f''(c) > 0 \) means bowl-shaped → minimum; \( f''(c) < 0 \) means dome-shaped → maximum; \( f''(c) = 0 \) → the test is silent, fall back on the first test.
The word-problem recipe: (1) translate into a formula, (2) note the domain, (3) solve \( f' = 0 \), (4) test candidates AND boundaries, (5) state the answer in a sentence with units.
When \( f' = 0 \) cannot be solved analytically: gradient descent — repeatedly step against the slope, \( x \leftarrow x - \eta f'(x) \). That is exactly how every ML model minimises its loss.

blocks.html: Every optimization problem has the same shape: an objective function (profit, volume, loss), choice variables and a domain of allowed choices. The calculus reflex: on a smooth function a peak or valley cannot be tilted — hence \( f'(c) = 0 \).

Local versus global: a local maximum only beats its immediate surroundings; a global one is the highest point of the entire domain. For convex functions (\( f'' \ge 0 \), like squared loss) they coincide — for non-convex ones (neural networks) they do not.
Terminology: extremum = umbrella term; critical point = interior candidate (\( f' = 0 \) or non-differentiable); inflection point = curvature sign change. And: max of \( f \) = min of \( -f \).

Collecting candidates is mechanical: differentiate, set to zero, solve. For \( f(x) = x^3 - 3x \): \( f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3 = 0 \) gives \( x = \pm 1 \). In the plot the yellow curve is \( f' \) — critical points sit exactly where it crosses the x-axis.

blocks.title: f and f′ in one view
blocks.subtitle: Slide xc along the cubic f(x) = x³ − 3x (cyan) and watch the slope chip move; the yellow curve is the derivative f′(x) = 3x² − 3. Where the yellow curve crosses the x-axis (x = −1 and x = 1) the slope is zero — those are the critical points. The status chip reads f′ as language.

blocks.html: Reading off: \( x = -1 \) is the top (\( f(-1) = 2 \), local max), \( x = 1 \) the bottom (\( f(1) = -2 \), local min). But at \( x = 0 \) the curve is horizontal-without-extremum: a critical point is a candidate, not a verdict.

sections.title: Rising, falling and the first test

blocks.html: The sign of \( f' \) is the complete motion description: positive = rising, negative = falling, zero = flat. Classification looks at what happens around the point — the first-derivative test.

Execution with a sign chart: zeros of \( f' \) in a row, one test point per interval, note the sign. For the cubic: rising on \( (-\infty, -1) \), falling on \( (-1, 1) \), rising on \( (1, \infty) \) — hill first, then valley.
For a global extremum on \( [a, b] \): evaluate \( f \) at the interior critical points plus both endpoints — the largest/smallest wins. Classic trap: forgetting the edges.

sections.title: Bending: concavity and the second test

blocks.html: Where \( f'' > 0 \) the function is convex (bowl-shaped), where \( f'' < 0 \) concave (hill-shaped), where the sign flips sits an inflection point. For \( x^3 - 3x \): \( f''(x) = 6x \) — inflection at the origin.

rows: local minimum — the lowest point of the bowl
local maximum — the top of the dome
test is silent — fall back on the first-derivative test

blocks.html: The second test is often faster: it only needs \( f'' \) at the critical point. Intuition: standstill (\( f' = 0 \)) plus positive acceleration = minimum; negative = maximum. Limitation: at \( f''(c) = 0 \) it says nothing (see \( x^4 \)).

For ML, concavity is the heart of learning: a convex loss has one valley (any descent strategy finds it), a non-convex one has several valleys and plateaus — and the learning rate is a concavity matter.

sections.title: A classic problem: the cardboard box

blocks.html: AP-style word problem: square cardboard 30×30 cm, cut an \( x \times x \) square from each corner, fold up the sides. Base \( (30-2x)^2 \), height \( x \), so \( V(x) = x(30-2x)^2 \) on the domain \( x \in (0, 15) \).

blocks.label: Box volume
blocks.caption: height × width × depth. A cubic function of the cut size — at both ends of the domain the volume goes to zero, so the maximum is guaranteed to sit inside.

blocks.html: Differentiate with the product rule: \( V'(x) = (30-2x)(30-6x) \). Zeros: \( x = 15 \) (edge, zero volume) and \( x = 5 \). Second test: \( V''(5) = -120 < 0 \) — maximum at \( x = 5 \), volume \( V(5) = 2000 \) cm³.

blocks.title: Volume against the cut size
blocks.subtitle: Slide the cut size x and hunt for the maximum: at x = 5 cm the volume chip lights up green — exactly the answer from the analysis. Note the slope chip V′: positive left of the maximum (more volume available), exactly zero at the top, negative after (you are cutting too much away).

blocks.html: In the plot: left of 5 \( V' > 0 \) (more volume), at 5 the slope is zero, right of it negative. Both physical edges are terrible (volume 0) — so the optimum must lie inside.
This pattern — edges terrible, interior smooth, hence critical point — is why optimization problems almost always take this shape. Whether a box or a loss landscape.

sections.title: Searching without a formula: gradient descent

blocks.html: Try solving \( f'(x) = 0 \) for a neural network's loss with a million weights: no closed form. So flip the approach: you do not need to know where the slope vanishes, only follow it — one step against the slope.

blocks.label: Gradient-descent update
blocks.caption: η (eta) is the learning rate: the step size. In higher dimensions f′ becomes the gradient ∇f and the rule stays literally the same — see Gradient descent.

blocks.html: Small example: \( f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 5 \), so \( f'(x) = 2x - 4 \), minimum at \( x = 2 \). Start \( x_0 = 5 \) with \( \eta = 0.1 \): every step \( x \leftarrow 0.8x + 0.4 \) — the distance to 2 shrinks by a factor 0.8 per step.

blocks.caption: gradient descent finds the parabola's minimum
blocks.source:
# f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 5  ->  f'(x) = 2x - 4  ->  minimum at x = 2
x, eta = 5.0, 0.1
for step in range(35):
    x = x - eta * (2*x - 4)     # one step against the slope
    if step % 5 == 0:
        print(f'step {step:2d}: x = {x:.4f}   f(x) = {x*x - 4*x + 5:.4f}')
print(f'after 35 steps: x = {x:.4f}  (exact minimum: x = 2)')

blocks.html: Typical output: 4.4000, 2.7864, 2.2577, 2.0844, 2.0277, 2.0091 — after 35 steps 2.0012. At \( \eta > 1 \) the sequence jumps everywhere: the divergence from Gradient descent, in miniature.

blocks.caption: the box problem numerically: scipy as a second opinion
blocks.source:
from scipy.optimize import minimize_scalar

def V(x):
    return x * (30 - 2*x)**2        # the box volume

# minimise -V on the physical domain (0, 15)
res = minimize_scalar(lambda x: -V(x), bounds=(0, 15), method='bounded')
print(f'optimum at x = {res.x:.4f} cm')
print(f'maximum volume  = {-res.fun:.1f} cm^3')
print('the analysis said: x = 5, V = 2000')

blocks.html: Typical output: x = 5.0000, V = 2000.0 — the numerical search engine and manual calculus agree. Analysis gives insight; scipy.optimize gives answers where algebra stalls.
The whole ML workflow in one breath: loss = objective, weights = knobs, gradient = derivative in many dimensions, and training = repeated \( x \leftarrow x - \eta \nabla f(x) \).
